audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-strict, word-initial primary accent, trochaic/dactylic secondaries) rests on the standard and only reference grammar, Hercus 1982 PL B-67, which we hold; the deciding passage was located verbatim at printed p.45 (pdf p.63) and the corr-note passage at p.47. Andersen 2015 (downloaded now) restates the same rule. No phonology article or instrumental study exists per Glottolog and web search. sources.citation: Andersen, Elena Handlos. 2015. Development of a Learner's Grammar for Paakantyi. MA thesis, University of Sydney (v+71+270 pp). USyd SeS handle 2123/14542 (could not be reached by automated download; archived copy (Internet Archive, 1 Apr 2022)).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'In Paakantyi, words with more than one syllable always have the main (primary) stress on the first syllable. In words with three or more syllables, there is also a weak (secondary) stress on the third syllable. For example, the word Paakantyi has primary stress on the first syllable and secondary stress on the third syllable.' Then quotes Hercus (2013:124-125) on emphatic/calling forms shifting stress to the last syllable.
sources.locator: Learner's Grammar §2.2 Stress, printed p.21 (pdf p.99); also §on clitics (-thinga attracts stress) and exclamations (final-syllable stress)
sources.note: Only post-1982 descriptive treatment; downloaded now, its §2.2 confirms initial primary stress with secondary on the third syllable (derived from Hercus).
